Topic Number: ARAS0015 Lost Communication Concerns with Autonomous Ground Vehicle Systems (AGVS) in the Airport Environment Technical POC: William Gorman; William.R.Gorman@faa.gov Copy: 9-ACT-AAQ-600-BAA@faa.gov Background: The integration of Autonomous Ground Vehicle Systems (AGVS) within the airport environment-both in the United States (U.S.) and internationally-has accelerated due to growing demands for efficiency and automation. Airports have begun testing a wide variety of AGVSs across various functions, including but not limited to self-driving jet bridges, aircraft tugs, baggage carts, de-icing vehicles, employee shuttles, mowers, foreign object debris collection, and perimeter inspections. Numerous airport sponsors and operators in the U.S. are testing/demonstrating AGVS with the intention of integrating them into their daily operations. The introduction of AGVS into the airport environment poses a new set of safety, integration, and validation challenges. One area of concern centers on the loss of communication between the command-and-control system (C2) monitored by a human-in-the-loop and the AGVS. This Broad Agency Announcement (BAA) topic is to address the need to better understand the circumstances regarding how to approach loss of communication issues with the introduction of AGVS into the airport environment. Purpose: The purpose of this topic is for interested p
[...]
 respective C2, monitored by a human-in-the-loop; where through different wireless platforms, commands may be issued to start or end specific tasks or abort the mission in the event of a problem. Due to the nature of wireless communication, this communication link may be lost at times, usually temporarily, but possibly for longer durations. o Identify (1) the varying processes AGVS companies currently follow and, where appropriate, (2) provide updates to existing processes or (3) recommend new processes that should be followed in the event of a lost link with AGVS operating in airport movement areas. Different lost link time durations (e.g., sporadic vs. longer term) and the purpose or AGVS vehicle type (e.g., mowers, luggage delivery, etc.) should be considered. o Research should consider vehicle behavior in the event of loss of communication -e.g., will the vehicle continue and complete its task, under what circumstances should the vehicle immediately stop, under what conditions should the vehicle go to a safe area, and when should the vehicle abort the mission and return to its home base location. o Provide innovative ideas to identify procedures to follow when the communication link is restored -e.g., remain stationary, resume the mission, move to a temporary safe location, or return to the home base location. Safety Analysis -Identify a safety analysis regarding the procedures and vehicle behavior in the event of lost communications. Period of Performance/Rough Order of Magnitude: The Period of Performance for projects under this topic is anticipated not to exceed 12 months. Numerous airport sponsors and operators in the U.S. are testing/demonstrating AGVS with the intention of integrating them into their daily operations. The introduction of AGVS into the airport environment poses a new set of safety, integration, and validation challenges. 5 BAA FAA Aviation Research 2025 Solicitation Number: 692M15-25-R-00004 One area of concern centers on the impact by AGVS on frequencies used by other airport equipment. This Broad Agency Announcement (BAA) topic is to address the need to better understand the possibility of spectrum interference associated with the introduction of AGVS into the airport environment. Purpose: The purpose of this topic is for interest
[...]
bility of spectrum interference associated with the introduction of AGVS into the airport environment. Purpose: The purpose of this topic is for interested parties to conduct applied research regarding innovative ways to better understand and mitigate potential spectrum interference risks in the airport environment due to the introduction of AGVS. Research will explore: (1) The spectrum impact that AGVS may introduce to FAA Navigational Aids (NAVAIDS)/airport equipment (e.g., avian radar, unmanned aircraft detection systems, foreign object debris detection systems, and other equipment) and (2) the spectrum impact that FAA NAVIDS/airport equipment may have on AGVS. Requirements: The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) seeks white papers to address the specific areas listed below; however, submittals are not limited to these areas. Identify Airport Risks o Propose a process identifying the list of frequencies used by AGVS, frequencies used by airport communication, navigation, and surveillance (CNS) infrastructure (e.g., with FAA NAVAIDS), and how to identify the spectrum interference risks to both FAA NAVAIDS/airport equipment and to the AGVS. The AGVS frequencies being employed may extend beyond just the vehicle and include related equipment (e.g., command and control equipment and vehicle communication devices). o Provide information regarding how to determine a governance policy to identify and address all spectrum interference issues Period of Performance/Rough Order of Magnitude: The Period of Performance for projects under this topic is anticipated not to exceed 12 months. 6 BAA FAA Aviation Research 2025 Solicitation Number: 692M15-25-R-00004 AIRPORT RESEARCH STRUCTURES AND MATERIALS (ARSM) Topic Number: ARSM0001: Structural Integrity of Metallic Components Technical POC: Dr. Edward Weinstein Edward.Weinstein@faa.gov Sohrob Mottaghi Sohrob.Mottaghi@faa.gov Copy: 9-ACT-AAQ-600-BAA@faa.gov Background: FAA Order 8110.107B prescribes the use of the Monitor Safety/Analyze Data (MSAD) process to make Continued Operational Safety (COS) decisions based on risk analysis methodologies. This order explains how the MSAD process analyzes COS data and monitors safety in aircraft fleets throughout their life cycle. The MSAD process helps the FAA identify hazards in in-service aircraft fleets and mitigate safety risks across the fleet by analyzing aviation safety data. MSAD also identifies other causes of hazards that cannot be addressed by aircraft fleet mitigations, such as issues related to product or part design or manufacturing. Additionally, MSAD discusses a datadriven, risk-based approach for follow-on actions, such as airworthiness directives (AD), special airworthiness information bulletins (SAIB), and others. Purpose: The purpose of this project is to obtain data that can be used in risk assessment and the development of guidance material for airplane structural integrity concerns in metallic structures of transport category airplanes, aligned with MSAD
